memory_update.text: Add MOD as a direct AI data-center cooling candidate; evidence strength is high because company materials explicitly reference hyperscale/colocation customers, data-center cooling growth, and liquid-cooling investment.
Add NVT as a direct power-plus-liquid-cooling infrastructure candidate; monitor conversion of announced AI data-center products and Siemens architecture collaboration into measurable revenue/backlog.
Add FIX and EME as scaled electrical/mechanical contracting candidates where skilled labor, prefabrication, and project execution can become AI data-center buildout chokepoints.

Add POWL as a smaller but still above-$1B-market-cap electrical-distribution/switchgear candidate; direct data-center share is not yet quantified, so keep as inference until backlog/end-market data confirms exposure.

Still need a separate pass on regulated utilities/IPPs, gas turbines, nuclear fuel, transformers, copper/cable, UPS/batteries, and data-center REIT/land-power asset owners to avoid over-weighting contractor/equipment names.

MOD should be added as a direct AI data-center thermal-management candidate; strongest public evidence is the $180M AI infrastructure cooling order and FY2025 annual-report language on high-density/liquid-cooling solutions.

BE should be added as a direct onsite-power candidate for grid-constrained AI data centers; evidence includes Equinix >100MW, AEP gigawatt procurement, Oracle deployment, and Brookfield AI infrastructure partnership.

HUBB should be tracked as an electrical/grid component supplier; evidence is less pure-play than MOD/BE but relevant to substations, connectors, electrical solutions, and AI data-center power distribution.
WCC should be tracked as a distributor/supply-chain coordinator for data-center electrical, communications, and utility products; 2025 data-center sales exposure appears material.
CAT should be tracked for behind-the-meter and backup power generation tied to AI data centers through engines, turbines, and collaborations with Vertiv and Hunt Energy.

The power/cooling/grid node has multiple scarcity subnodes: liquid cooling, onsite generation, substation/electrical components, distribution logistics, switchgear/transformers, and EPC/grid construction. This pass added candidates mainly in cooling, onsite power, components, and distribution.

Further passes should verify additional US-listed candidates in cables/copper, switchgear, backup power, battery storage, building controls, water treatment, gas supply, and regulated utilities/IPPs with signed hyperscaler PPAs or large-load agreements.
Add MOD as a direct data-center thermal-management candidate; focus next checks on data-center cooling backlog, liquid-cooling mix, and capacity constraints.
Add NVT as a rack-level power plus liquid-cooling candidate; its exposure sits near the interface of chip thermal requirements and facility deployment.
Add FIX as a mechanical/electrical contracting and skilled-labor execution candidate for AI data-center construction.
Add WCC as a second-order electrical and network infrastructure distributor/logistics candidate; watch margins and working-capital intensity.
Add GNRC as an underappreciated backup-power and integrated-energy candidate tied to data-center reliability and grid interconnection delays.

Bloom Energy, Powell Industries, Atkore, Hubbell, Belden, Dycom, EMCOR, MasTec, AECOM, Fluor, and selected utilities/IPPs remain candidates for a later pass if the dashboard needs more coverage across onsite power, switchgear, conduit, grid construction, EPC, and regulated generation.

For this node, the key falsification signals are backlog cancellations, hyperscaler capex pauses, falling transformer/switchgear/cooling lead times, margin compression from capacity additions, permitting restrictions on diesel/gas backup power, and evidence that AI rack-density improvements reduce facility-level power and cooling intensity.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the universe around the AI data-center power/cooling/grid node with five US-listed direct or second-order infrastructure names beyond the obvious hyperscaler/semiconductor layer. The highest-fit additions are concentrated in thermal equipment, liquid-cooling components, electrical/mechanical contracting, and custom power-distribution equipment. This is research support only, not a buy/sell recommendation. Expanded the US-listed universe for the AI data-center power/cooling/grid node beyond the seed list. The strongest incremental candidates are direct suppliers of thermal systems, onsite power, electrical components, and distribution/supply-chain capacity. The node remains framed as a hypothesis: after accelerators are procured, deployment can be constrained by deliverable power, substations, switchgear, UPS, transformers, cooling, permitting, and time-to-power. No trading recommendation is implied. Expanded the US-listed universe toward less obvious second-order beneficiaries tied to AI data-center power and thermal constraints. The highest-relevance additions are companies exposed to liquid cooling, rack-level power distribution, mechanical/electrical contracting, electrical-products distribution/logistics, and backup/onsite power. These are not buy/sell recommendations; they are research candidates for further evidence collection around backlog, data-center revenue mix, lead times, hyperscaler qualification, margin sustainability, and whether AI-driven demand is already priced in.
